name: Wei Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Wei. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in recoveries at a big insurer's head office, which means chasing money back. When our customer's car gets hit and we pay out, I go after the other driver's insurer to get our money back. It's evidence, letters, deadlines and haggling. I run every file through an AI tool first to pull out the dates, the damage figures and who was at fault, then I write the demand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy winning. Getting a stubborn insurer to pay the full amount feels like closing a deal. What wears me out is the waiting, months for a reply sometimes. Outside work, my brother and I own a small flat we rent out, and I help my dad at his hardware shop on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would surprise me. I see what these tools do every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good and the people who learned them came out ahead. I'd say the market sorted out the hype, which it usually does. At church I'd keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep a good job where I'm faster than most, and my recovery numbers stay high. If AI stalls here, the clerk who already uses it every morning just keeps beating the clerks who don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, push for a promotion based on my numbers, and put the bonus into a second rental flat with my brother. I'd keep helping at the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I like where these tools were going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your numbers compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I close about a third more files than the team average. My manager knows it's the tool, and I don't hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that worries you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Interest rates for the flat, maybe. That's about it.

I'd say the **market** sorted out the hype, as it usually does.
think: I keep a **good job** where I'm faster than most.
My **recovery numbers** stay high thanks to the tools.
do: Push for a **promotion** based on my numbers.
Put the bonus into a **second rental flat** with my brother.
feel: **Calm**, a little **flat** that the tools stalled.
S0.quote: If AI stalls here, the clerk who already uses it every morning just keeps beating the clerks who don't.
fieldNote: Wei sees AI as a **competitive edge** he already holds.
His **rental flat** gives him a second income.
His only standing worry is **interest rates**.

steps.text: Ask for a promotion using his recovery numbers
Buy a second rental flat with his brother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I'd actually welcome, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how progress works: some jobs go, new ones come, and people should get on with learning. At work I'd offer to show the team how I use the tools. I wouldn't call for government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm one of the winners. The recoveries team shrinks, but someone has to run the tools and handle the hard negotiations. In a recoveries team that shrinks by half, I plan to be the one who teaches the software where to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the automation of our recovery process, and get paid for it. I'd keep investing in property with my brother. I'd also think about starting a small business helping firms automate their paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sorry for the colleagues who'd struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karen, who's been there twenty years. She's good, but she writes everything by hand first. I'd try to help her, but I can't make her learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no government help. What about Karen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her family, her church, her savings. And the company could help with training. I don't think the state should pay people to not change.

fieldNote: Wei's **free-market** view makes him welcome the change.
He'd rather **family and church** catch people than the state.
He sees a **business opportunity** in others' automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here and we should adapt fast, not ask for handouts. With my dad I'd say the shop is suddenly the safest part of the family. I'd still not campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my edge disappears within a year or two. If a machine thinks like a person, it doesn't need me to steer it. Being ahead of everyone on AI only matters while the AI needs someone ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more money into the rental flats and the shop, since those don't depend on my desk job. I'd learn the hardware trade properly from my dad, because hands-on work gets three more years. And I'd keep the insurance job until they let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not broke, but my plan would need to change fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your side business idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dead. If AGI does it all, firms don't need me to help them automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the hardware shop really safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few years. People still want someone to tell them which screw to use. After the robots, who knows.

I'd tell my dad the **shop** is now the family's safest part.
think: My **edge disappears** within a year or two.

do: Put more money into the **rental flats** and the shop.

Keep the **insurance job** until they let me go.
feel: **Anxious**: not broke, but his plan must **change fast**.
S2.quote: Being ahead of everyone on AI only matters while the AI needs someone ahead of it.
fieldNote: Wei's AI edge **evaporates** under fast AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Good. That I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's not panic and let's learn. At church I'd tell the young lads to learn a trade too. Online I'd share tools, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get three or four very good years leading automation, earn well, and build up property. Then I'd move into the shop. Five years of good wages from automating insurance is the money that buys my next life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the automation lead role, save hard, and buy the second flat. I'd start learning the shop properly in year two or three. I'd stay at the insurer until year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the insurer early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if they stopped paying me well. Until then, it's the best money I can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let's buy the second flat now, before every other clerk in the city has the same idea.

I'd tell young lads at church to learn a **trade**.
think: I'd get **three or four** good years leading automation.
Those wages buy my **next life** in property and the shop.
do: Take the **automation lead** role and save hard.

S3.quote: Five years of good wages from automating insurance is the money that buys my next life.
fieldNote: Wei treats five years as a **window to earn** before switching.
He'd move fast on **property** before others catch on.
Faith and **trade** both shape his advice to young people.

steps.text: Take the automation lead role and save the extra pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for anyone willing to work. At work I'd train people. At church I'd keep encouraging the young ones to learn useful things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I ride it well: years of automation work, more flats, and maybe I take over the shop when dad retires. Ten years is enough to become the guy who automated the insurer and then the guy who owns the hardware shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead automation at work, keep buying property, and plan to take over the shop around year seven. I'd keep my faith and my family close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Property prices, if everyone loses jobs at once. That's my blind spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger version of yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade and the tools at the same time. Don't pick one.

say: I'd call it an **opportunity** for anyone willing to work.
I'd **train people** at work and encourage young ones at church.
think: I **ride it well** with automation work and property.
I might take over **the shop** when Dad retires.
do: Plan to take over the **hardware shop** around year seven.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to become the guy who automated the insurer and then the guy who owns the hardware shop.
fieldNote: Wei sees a ten-year runway as **opportunity**, not threat.
His blind spot is **property prices** if jobs vanish widely.
He blends **trade and tools**, fitting his traditional and adaptive mix.

steps.text: Lead automation work at the insurer
Keep buying rental property with his brother
Take over the family hardware shop around year seven

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my edge disappears overnight. What would help is clear rules so businesses can plan, and cheap trade training. I don't need anyone to save me; I need the rules to stay clear long enough for me to make my next move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. The old hardware shop might outlast my whole insurance career.

portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** recoveries clerk at a big insurer's head office.
He uses **AI tools daily** and closes a third more files than average.
He owns a **rental flat** with his brother and helps at his dad's hardware shop.
He's **free-market** and wants family, church and companies, not the state, to catch people.
He's **calm** in most pictures, uneasy in AGI by 2031 and **anxious** in AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his AI edge disappears overnight.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **rules** for business planning and cheap **trade training**.
